strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP-for-code problem with a coherent workflow integrating fault localization, patch generation, test feedback, and repository analysis. Escalating to more extensive analysis after failed repairs is a reasonable design.

The reported results are promising: 197 correct Defects4J repairs versus ChatRepair’s 157, complete QuixBugs repair, and consistent improvements across seven backbones for FixAgent-Lite on 600 ConDefects examples. Four benchmarks and three programming languages provide useful evaluation breadth.

The manuscript supplies agent prompts, workflow diagrams, pseudocode, and a source-code link. It distinguishes plausible from correct patches and replaces unrestricted web retrieval with a local corpus during evaluation to reduce direct solution leakage.
weaknesses: The correctness evidence needs auditing. Appendix A.4 presents Figure 24 as a successful repair, but its boundary checks examine the last significant hexadecimal digit rather than the first. For 0x80000000, the printed patch still calls createInteger, reproducing the overflow failure; Figure 17 explicitly expects a Long. This does not establish that the aggregate counts are wrong, but the contradiction is material, particularly because the procedure and criteria used to adjudicate the 197 correct repairs are not adequately documented.

The end-to-end claim depends on an underspecified initial localization step. Section 3.1 and Algorithm 1 require metadata containing the bug-located file. Although the text says this file is identified through testing, it does not specify a reproducible selection procedure or treatment of incorrect selections and multiple candidate files. Consequently, the evaluation does not clearly establish the claimed absence of prior fault-localization assistance.

The ablations do not isolate the contribution of hierarchical coordination. Table 2 progressively adds agents, information, tools, and computation. A comparison against a single agent with equivalent tools and budget, or an alternative workflow using the same components, is needed to attribute improvements to the proposed organization. Moreover, the seven-backbone experiment evaluates Lite, which omits much of the full hierarchy.

The superiority and efficiency claims exceed the comparative evidence. Table 1 combines historical results with different backbones, localization assumptions, benchmark coverage, and sampling budgets. A framework attempt can involve several model calls and patch candidates, so comparing 20 attempts with another method’s patch samples does not establish lower cost. Table 2’s expense per run does not resolve total expenditure or runtime under the complete retry policy.

Several quantitative inconsistencies require reconciliation: Table 1 reports 286 plausible Defects4J repairs, whereas Tables 2 and 4 report 291 for the complete system; RewardRepair has 90 correct but only 75 plausible repairs; and Codeflaws contains 3,902 bugs in the setup but 3,982 in the results. These may be reporting errors, but they prevent an unambiguous interpretation of the evaluation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful prompts and code link. The manuscript does not adequately specify exact model versions, decoding settings, sampling seeds, the per-agent retry limit m, or local retrieval configuration and overlap checks. Algorithm 1 also returns unconditionally inside its outer attempt loop, conflicting with the described repeated attempts. These fixable validation and reporting gaps currently prevent a clear Findings recommendation; targeted verification and controlled comparisons could support resubmission next cycle.
